response:
Orientation

The central question is: when you merge two or more fine-tuned models using task-vector arithmetic (e.g., adding the delta between a fine-tuned and base model back onto a base), do the causal mechanisms responsible for a specific capability survive intact — or do they relocate, fragment, or silently degrade even when behavioral outputs look fine on benchmarks?

Task-vector arithmetic rests on a linearity assumption: that capabilities decompose additively in weight space. Causal tracing (à la ROME/MEMIT-style path patching) probes where in a network a fact or skill is computed — typically identifying which MLP layers or attention heads are causally decisive. The worry is that merging can preserve the output distribution of a capability while scrambling its internal causal structure, producing a model that answers correctly for the wrong reasons, with fragile generalization.

The multilingual dimension sharpens this considerably. Multilingual fine-tuning already produces models where the same semantic computation may be distributed differently across languages — some capabilities appear to route through a shared "language-neutral" substrate, others stay language-specific. When you merge a multilingual model with a task-specialized one, you're composing two distinct causal topologies, and there's no guarantee the merged weight interpolation preserves either topology faithfully.

What a beginner misses is that benchmark accuracy is nearly useless as a fidelity signal here. A model can achieve 90% accuracy on a task post-merge while the causal pathway that was doing the work has been disrupted and a shallower, more brittle heuristic has taken over — something causal tracing would reveal but held-out accuracy never would.

response:
Relocation vs. Destruction in Path-Patching Signatures

In standard causal tracing (Meng et al., 2022 — the ROME paper), a "causal hotspot" manifests as a sharp peak in indirect effect when you restore a corrupted run's activations at a specific (layer, position) site; the peak is typically narrow — in GPT-2 XL, factual recall concentrates in a 2–3 layer window around layers 13–17 of the MLP stream. Relocation would show up as that peak flattening at its original site while a new peak emerges elsewhere — total indirect effect is conserved (the model still does the task), but the mass has shifted, say, from mid-layer MLPs to late-layer attention heads. Destruction looks different: the indirect effect profile goes flat or diffuse everywhere — no single site recovers performance when restored, meaning the computation has become distributed below detectability or has genuinely been ablated, and corrupted-vs-clean performance gap collapses toward zero. The diagnostic crux is therefore whether the sum of indirect effects across all sites remains roughly constant post-merge (relocation) or drops substantially (destruction). A subtler signal that experts watch for: relocation often produces a wider peak with lower maximum but equivalent integral, because the merged weights spread the computation across more layers — this can masquerade as partial destruction if you only inspect peak height rather than the full area-under-curve of the indirect effect distribution. Wang et al.'s IOI circuit work (2022) established that attention heads can fully absorb tasks previously handled by MLPs under fine-tuning pressure, so the relocation scenario is mechanistically plausible, not merely theoretical.

Cross-Lingual Causal Signal After Monolingual Task-Vector Merge

The empirical expectation, grounded in work by Wendler et al. (2024, "Do Llamas Work in English?") and related probing studies, is that multilingual transformers perform a implicit language pivoting step — non-English inputs are re-encoded into a language-neutral (often English-skewed) representational substrate in middle layers before task computation fires, then decoded back into the target language in late layers. When you merge a monolingual English task vector into this system, causal tracing on a non-English prompt will typically show the task-relevant indirect effect signal surviving in the middle-layer MLP hotspot — because that's where the language-neutral substrate lives and where the task vector's weight delta lands — but the late-layer attention heads responsible for language-appropriate output formatting show degraded or mislocated indirect effect, since the monolingual task vector never trained those heads for non-English generation. The reveal is significant: task vectors are not uniformly distributed across the residual stream but are disproportionately encoded in the language-neutral middle-layer MLPs, which is why the merged model can often retrieve the right answer concept cross-lingually but then fails at surface realization — outputting English, code-switching, or producing fluent but wrong-register text in the target language. This dissociation — intact semantic causal hotspot, broken output-language causal hotspot — is something aggregate accuracy metrics completely miss, because a partial-credit scorer may reward the semantic content while the language fidelity failure goes unmeasured. Concretely, in mBERT and early mT5 analyses, the middle 40–60% of layers showed the strongest cross-lingual alignment (Pires et al., 2019; Conneau et al., 2020), and those are precisely the layers where task-vector arithmetic does its heaviest lifting — making them the load-bearing zone for both the capability and its cross-lingual transfer, and the first place a careful experimenter should run differential path-patching between the pre- and post-merge models.

response:
Interference Structure When Two Task Vectors Collide in the Same Zone

The answer is neither purely constructive nor purely destructive — Ilharco et al. (2023, "Editing Models with Task Arithmetic") and the follow-up TIES-merging paper (Yadav et al., 2023) both document that when two task vectors have opposing signs on the same parameters, they cancel, but when they have concordant signs, they can amplify — however, this sign-level analysis obscures a more structured phenomenon that causal tracing exposes. What actually happens in the middle-layer MLPs is best described as causal basis interference: each task vector implicitly defines a low-dimensional subspace of weight-space in which its causal computation lives, and when two such subspaces have high cosine overlap (which they will if both are doing language-neutral semantic retrieval), the merged model's indirect effect for each task gets projected onto the union of both subspaces, producing cross-task "crosstalk" — restoring activations for task A's corrupted run partially recovers task B's output as well, a signature that the causal circuits are no longer orthogonal. TIES-merging's core fix — trimming low-magnitude deltas and resolving sign conflicts before summing — partially addresses destructive interference but does nothing about this subspace overlap problem, which is a geometric issue, not a sign issue. Ortiz Jimenez et al. (2023, "Task Arithmetic in the Tangent Space") showed that merging in the tangent space of a linearized model improves separability, implicitly because tangent-space projections better respect the local curvature that keeps task subspaces apart — this is the closest the literature has come to directly addressing causal basis interference. The practical implication for causal tracing fidelity is grim: two tasks that are behaviorally compatible (no output conflict) can still be causally entangled post-merge, meaning that ablating one task's circuit will unpredictably damage the other's, and this entanglement scales with the degree of middle-layer weight-space overlap between the two fine-tuning runs.

response:
Pre-Merge Diagnostics for Causal Entanglement

The most principled existing tool is singular subspace overlap between the two task-vector matrices restricted to the middle-layer MLPs: compute the SVD of each task vector's weight delta (reshaped as a matrix per layer), take the top-k singular vectors, and measure the principal angles between the two subspaces — small principal angles mean high overlap and predicted causal entanglement. Gravity et al. and the DARE paper (Yu et al., 2023) implicitly use magnitude-based sparsification as a proxy for this, but magnitude is a poor surrogate for subspace geometry; two task vectors can have large, non-overlapping singular subspaces (safe to merge) or small, highly aligned ones (dangerous) regardless of their parameter magnitudes. A more predictive diagnostic emerges from Fisher Information overlap: the Fisher diagonal for each fine-tuned model, estimated on a small calibration set, identifies which parameters are causally load-bearing for each task, and the dot product of the two Fisher vectors over the middle-layer MLP parameters gives a scalar that directly predicts interference — this is the core insight behind EWC (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017) repurposed as a merge compatibility score rather than a regularizer. Konkretely, if you threshold Fisher overlap above ~0.3 (on a normalized scale) for the middle 40% of layers, you should predict substantial causal fidelity loss; below ~0.1, merging is likely safe — these thresholds are rough extrapolations from continual learning results but have not been formally validated in the task-arithmetic merging literature, which is itself a gap. The fundamental limitation of all pre-merge diagnostics is that they measure weight-space overlap as a proxy for activation-space causal overlap, and these can diverge: two task vectors can occupy orthogonal weight subspaces yet produce highly correlated middle-layer activations due to the nonlinearity of the forward pass, meaning a truly reliable pre-merge diagnostic may require running cheap forward passes on probe inputs rather than relying on weight geometry alone.

The Weight-Safe / Activation-Dangerous Adversarial Case

Construct two task vectors as follows: Task A fine-tunes on a relation that requires the MLP at layer L to implement a specific input-gated computation — the weight delta is small but the function it performs is highly nonlinear, activating only when the residual stream carries a particular feature direction v. Task B fine-tunes on a superficially unrelated task whose weight delta, also small and orthogonal to Task A's in weight space, happens to rotate the residual stream at layer L-1 such that v is now present for Task B's inputs as well. Every weight-space metric — Fisher overlap, singular subspace principal angles, TIES sign conflict rate — reads near zero because the deltas genuinely are orthogonal; yet post-merge, Task B's inputs now route through Task A's nonlinear gate at layer L, producing catastrophic cross-task activation interference invisible to any weight-space diagnostic. This is not merely a thought experiment: it is structurally identical to what Henighan et al. and the superposition literature (Elhage et al., 2022, "Toy Models of Superposition") describe when features are polysemantically encoded — a weight direction that is "inert" for one distribution becomes "live" for another when the input geometry shifts, and merging shifts the effective input geometry by superimposing two fine-tuning distributions. The deeper revelation is that weight-space merging theory is fundamentally a first-order theory applied to a second-order problem: task vectors capture where weights moved, but causal fidelity depends on how activations flow through those weights under the merged model's input distribution, which is a function of the interaction between both task vectors and the base model's nonlinearities simultaneously. This exposes a hard epistemological limit: you cannot fully predict merge safety from weights alone without either (a) linearizing the model — which is exactly what Ortiz Jimenez et al.'s tangent-space approach attempts, accepting approximation error — or (b) running forward passes, which collapses the diagnostic into a behavioral test and abandons the promise of weight-space prediction entirely. The practical implication is that any merge safety guarantee derived purely from weight geometry is, at best, a first-order approximation that breaks precisely in the high-stakes cases where tasks share input manifold geometry despite having orthogonal weight deltas — and multilingual models are especially vulnerable because their middle layers are designed to collapse diverse input distributions onto a shared manifold, maximizing the probability of exactly this adversarial geometry.

Exploiting the Shared Manifold for Causally Faithful Merging

The core idea is to treat the language-neutral manifold not as a liability but as a controlled routing substrate: if you can identify the principal directions of that manifold (via PCA or ICA on middle-layer activations across languages), you can decompose each task vector into a component within the manifold and a component orthogonal to it, then merge only the within-manifold components additively while keeping orthogonal components separate — a structured merge that respects the manifold's geometry rather than ignoring it. This is conceptually related to what Guillermo Ortiz-Jimenez et al. gesture at in tangent-space arithmetic, but the key difference is that the relevant tangent space here is not the model's full parameter tangent space but specifically the activation manifold tangent space at the middle layers, which you can estimate cheaply from a multilingual probe corpus without full linearization. Konkrete evidence that this is feasible comes from Zhao et al. (2024, "LORA-the-Explorer") and related LoRA merging work showing that when fine-tuning is constrained to low-rank subspaces aligned with dominant singular directions of the base model's weight matrices, merging interference drops substantially — the alignment to pre-existing structure is doing exactly this manifold-respecting routing implicitly. The design principle that follows is: fine-tune task vectors using activation-space regularization that penalizes deviation from the shared manifold's principal directions, so that each task vector learns to write its causal computation along manifold directions rather than across them, making the subsequent merge a nearly orthogonal addition in the space that actually matters for forward-pass behavior. Anthropic's representation engineering work (Zou et al., 2023) and the concept-vector literature more broadly suggest that many high-level semantic computations already live in low-dimensional linear subspaces of the residual stream — meaning the manifold has exploitable structure, it is not merely a dense blob, and task vectors designed to align with these semantic subspaces would be both more mergeable and more causally interpretable post-merge.

response:
The Expressive Power / Merge Fidelity Tradeoff and Unlearnability

The tradeoff is formally analogous to the bias-variance decomposition but in function space: constraining task vectors to the manifold's top-k principal directions reduces the effective parameter count available for task-specific computation, and for tasks whose optimal solution requires weight changes that are intrinsically orthogonal to the shared manifold, this constraint introduces irreducible bias — the model asymptotes to a performance ceiling below what unconstrained fine-tuning achieves regardless of data volume. The unlearnability regime is not merely theoretical: tasks that require language-specific phonological, morphological, or script-level processing are strong candidates, because these computations are precisely what the language-neutral manifold was trained to suppress during multilingual pre-training — the manifold's principal directions point away from language-specific variance by construction, so constraining fine-tuning to those directions would prevent the model from learning, say, Korean honorific agreement or Arabic root-and-pattern morphology at the level of causal precision those tasks demand. Quantitatively, the LoRA literature gives a useful proxy: Hu et al. (2021) showed that rank-4 to rank-64 adaptations span a wide performance range on GLUE, with diminishing returns above rank-32 for most tasks, but Peng et al. and subsequent multilingual LoRA analyses found that morphologically complex languages require significantly higher rank to match full fine-tuning — suggesting that the manifold-aligned subspace for those languages is intrinsically higher-dimensional, and a fixed low-rank manifold constraint will hit an expressive ceiling earlier. The precise crossover point — where merge fidelity gains from manifold constraint are outweighed by task-specific expressive loss — depends on the principal angle between the task's optimal update direction and the manifold, a quantity you can measure pre-training by running a small unconstrained fine-tuning pilot and projecting the resulting task vector onto the manifold basis; if the projection captures less than ~60-70% of the delta's variance, manifold-constrained merging will likely sacrifice too much task performance to be worthwhile. The deeper theoretical point is that multilingual pre-training has already made a lossy compression decision about what structure to share versus suppress, and manifold-constrained task vectors are forced to respect that prior decision — meaning the unlearnability regime is not a bug of the merging approach but a delayed consequence of the pre-training objective's own inductive biases, surfaced only when you try to merge.
